We give here the translation of this passage (Majlisî, pp. 146–147): “I said: ‘My lord, I find that some of the verses have no connection either with what comes before or with what follows them. My limited understanding cannot penetrate the reason.’ ‘Indeed,’ the Sayyed replied, ‘things are as you observe. The reason is this. When the prince of humankind (the Prophet), Mohammad ibn 'Abdillah, passed from this perishable dwelling to the everlasting Dwelling, and the two men of the Quraysh (the first two Sunni caliphs, Abû Bakr and 'Omar) did what they did, seizing the outward and public caliphate by force, the Commander of the Faithful (the First Imam) gathered the whole Quran into a leather covering and brought it to them while the Quraysh were assembled in the mosque. He said: “This is the Book of God which the Messenger of God commanded me to present to you, so that, on the Day of Resurrection, a witness may rise before God to testify against you.” But the Pharaoh and Nimrod of this community (that is, Caliph 'Omar ibn al-Khattâb) answered: “We have no need of your Quran.” The Imam replied: “The Messenger of God, my dearest friend, foretold that you would give me this answer. Yet I wished, by doing this, to bring forth testimony against you.” And the Commander of the Faithful returned to his home, saying: “There is no God but You, You alone. You have no partner. No one can overturn what has always been within Your knowledge, or oppose what Your wisdom requires. So be Yourself the Witness who will testify on my behalf against them on the Day of Resurrection.” Then Ibn Abî Qahâfa summoned the Muslims and said to them: “Whoever has in his possession a verse or a sura of the Quran, let him bring it here.” Then came Abû 'Obaydallah, 'Othmân, Mo'awiya, and others [...]. Each brought a verse or a sura, and from these they assembled the Quran we now have. But they left out everything that would have proved the wrongs they had committed since the Prophet's death. This is why the verses are not connected with one another. As for the Quran which the Commander of the Faithful compiled in his own handwriting, that is preserved with the Sâhib al-Amr (the Hidden Imam). It contains everything, absolutely everything. Nevertheless, concerning the Quran in our hands, there must be no doubt of its validity, nor of its being truly the Word of God. What I have just said I transmit exactly as it came from the Imam.’” ↩

Here are the details of the episode. The mysterious horseman says to 'Alî ibn Fâzel: “Spend the night with the people who live there. Tell them what religion you were born into. Did not everything happen exactly so, O Ibn Fâzel?” “I said: ‘Indeed it did! I went to the people of that village. I spent the night with them, and they showed me every courtesy. I asked them about their religion. They answered, without the slightest taqîyeh toward me: “We follow the religion of the Commander of the Faithful, heir of the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and of the Immaculate Imams descended from him.” I asked them: “How did this religion reach you? Who brought it to you?” They replied: “Abû Dharr al-Ghaffârî (one of the Prophet's companions), when 'Othmân (the third Sunni caliph) exiled him from Medina to Syria, and then Mo'awiya exiled him from Damascus to this country of ours. His spiritual influence extends to us all.” When morning came, I asked them to help me rejoin my caravan, and I in turn told them my religion. They provided two men who guided me back to my caravan.’” ↩

Let us recall the essential point about this word, used frequently throughout the present work. Imaginal (Latin imaginalis) derives from imago, like other words formed in the same way (compare derivatives of origo: originarius, originalis, etc.). Latin distinguishes imaginare, to present an image as a mirror presents it (the function expressed by Arabic mazharîya, and above all the nature of the 'âlam al-Mithâl, mundus imaginalis), from the deponent verb imaginari, to imagine or picture something to oneself. ↩

See our Avicenne et le Récit visionnaire, vol. I, pp. 18, 27, 31. We must distinguish the fact of exitus (departure) from spiritual death. If exitus is to be a real “departure” from this world, spiritual resurrection must have preceded it. Otherwise, those who are spiritually dead—that is, dead in the true sense—will never “leave” this world. Their exitus is only entry into the “second death,” for only those who are truly “alive” depart from this world. This teaching appears both in the Gospel of Philip and in an Ismaili treatise by Nasîroddîn Tûsî. Indeed, the entire spiritual education of Ismaili gnosis is founded on the “resurrection of the dead” (see Kitâb al-'âlim wa'l-gholâm, Annuaire, 1970–1971, pp. 226 ff.). He answered yes, and told me that down here in Strasbourg he had had the very same dream that I had had up above (in the Highlands).” The Friend of God then explains how both men came to conclude that “the time for building new cloisters had passed,” before continuing: “Then, the following Christmas night, at midnight on that holy night of Christ, we both—he below and I above—felt at the same time, in our nature (that is, in our bodies), such pain and suffering that we each imagined ourselves at the point of death. And in this suffering we received a revelation, so clear that it could only be believed, that we must found a cloister in Strasbourg. Thus the Green Island came into being” (ibid., p. 53). ↩

Ibid., pp. 53–55. Hélyot's Dictionnaire des Ordres religieux ou Histoire des Ordres monastiques, religieux et militaires, vol. II (Migne, Encyclopédie théologique, vol. XXI), Paris, 1848, cols. 855 ff., gives an entirely outward, historical account of the Green Island. He knows Rulman Merswin's role well but does not mention the Friend of God. After completely restoring the Green Island, Rulman Merswin “gave it to the Order of St John of Jerusalem on condition that the chaplain brothers of that Order would celebrate the divine office there in perpetuity. This donation was accepted by Conrad de Brunsberg, Grand Prior of Germany, and later confirmed by Grand Master Raymond Bérenger and the general chapter.” Raymond Bérenger, from the Dauphiné, was the Order's thirty-second Grand Master (d. 1373). ↩

Ibid., p. 55. Letters and short works written respectively by the Friend of God and Rulman Merswin were carefully collected and copied by the brothers of St John into magnificent manuscripts. Treasured within the Order as sacred relics, these are the source of what we know about the Friend of God. In brief, the collection comprises (1) the “Great German Memorial” (Das grosse deutsche Memorial), of which a Latin translation was made but has not survived; (2) the “Master's Book” (Das Meisterbuch), a collection of illustrated documents owned by Grand Prior Conrad von Brunsberg but now lost; and (3) the “Book of Letters” (Das Briefbuch). See W. Rath's description of the surviving Strasbourg manuscripts, op. cit., pp. 119–127. Nearly all this material has been published and, to some extent, translated, but unfortunately it is scattered through unrelated books that are now unobtainable. There is an urgent need to bring it together in one corpus, with the original texts and full translations. Several scholars have attempted to pierce the Friend of God's “anonymity,” identifying him, for example, with Nicholas of Basel. We believe these attempts to identify the historical individual have taken the wrong path; in any case, they fall outside our present concern. ↩
Ibid., p. 85. Here we can only allude to the mysterious scene of mutual recognition, almost as between initiates, that occurred when the Friend of God and two companions visited Pope Gregory XI. ↩

This mysterious union of “the fire from above” and “the fire from below” recalls an equally strange experience described by Najmoddîn Kobrâ, who sums it up in these words: “Whenever a flame rises from you, behold, a flame descends from Heaven toward you.” 'Aynol-Qozât Hamadânî (d. 525/1131), Ahmad Ghazâlî's favorite disciple, experienced the same conjunction of two lights. Hélyot's Dictionnaire (above, p. 399, n. 77), cols. 857 ff., continues an entirely outward history of the Green Island commandery (to which the commandery of Sélestat was subordinate): its destruction in 1633 and the compensations then granted to the Knights of St John, which remained in force until the Revolution. Nor do we need to consider here the later history of the Sovereign Order of St John of Jerusalem: the failure, if not betrayal, of Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch, who handed Malta over to Bonaparte; the knights' election of Tsar Paul I as Grand Master, by which the Order became ipso facto an “ecumenical religion”; or the papal order known as the “Order of Malta,” which was in fact newly created by a motu proprio of Pope Pius VII in 1803. ↩

See Ernst Benz, “Der Montserrat in der europäischen Geschichte,” in Zeitschrift für Religions- und Geistesgeschichte, XVIII, 1966, no. 1, pp. 15 ff. (Montserrat with its twelve hermitages!). The connection between Montserrat and classical Weimar began when Wilhelm von Humboldt described his ascent of that mountain as a completion of the Stimmung, the mood or emotional atmosphere to which Goethe had given form in his poem Die Geheimnisse. Goethe later forgot that he had learned of Montserrat only some twenty years after composing the unfinished poem, and then through Humboldt's description. Hence his reply to the Göttingen students who questioned him about the poem in 1816: Goethe retrospectively felt that he had already seen the description of Montserrat at the time. That impression was doubtless mistaken chronologically, but it had a deeper truth—the same truth that allows us to recognize the same mystical mountain in Montserrat, Montsalvat, and Montségur. For the ubi (the “where”) of Mount Qâf is an ubique (“everywhere”), and that “everywhere” is the place where the Hidden Imam manifests himself. (We intentionally retain the etymological two-word spelling in our text.) ↩

Hosayn Kâshefî, Fotowwat-Nâmeh, fols. 12b–13a. While Adam's other sons devote themselves to crafts that will enable them to gain the world, Seth dedicates himself wholly to divine service. The angel Gabriel brings from paradise a green (sabz) woolen (sûf) robe and clothes Seth in it. The angels visit him, then return to heaven and announce to the others: there is someone “clothed in wool” (sâfî) who devotes himself to divine service on earth! Thus, from the time of the prophet Seth, the name “those clothed in wool” is given to the group called “Sufis.” This tale illustrates the most common explanation of the word Sufi. Bîrûnî proposed another, connecting Arabic sufi with Greek sophos. ↩
